b: In its heyday, Shaw Brothers Studio’s focus on period-set genre films was a pragmatic move to appeal not only to Hong Kongers but audiences across Asia. Nonetheless, the studio did branch out into present-day action cinema in the 1970s, laying the groundwork for the Hong Kong New Wave with films that captured the region’s culture clashes between Eastern and Western authorities, its fluid sense of identity, and its criminal underworld.

Arrow’s latest collection of Shaw Brothers films gathers seven works from this side of the studio’s output, starting with 1973’s The Delinquent. In it, Shen Chang (Wong Chung), a scrappy, impoverished delivery boy, is groomed by gangsters into abetting their robbery of the warehouse where his father (Lu Ti) works as a guard. Co-directed by Shaw legends Chang Cheh and Kuei Chih-hung and choreographed by the great Lau Kar-leung, the film comes freighted with expectations that its first hour largely shirks, unfolding instead as a slow-burn youth-in-crisis drama that devotes far more attention to Hong Kong’s crowded streets and stark class stratification than to the short bursts of violence that Shen commits in fits of pique.

The last half hour, though, explodes into a frenzy of classic Chang Cheh action as Shen, fed up with being used by the triads, pursues revenge with suicidal intensity. The violence spills into ever stranger environments, at one point leaving our hero strapped to a sawmill log, contorting his body to avoid a blade poised to bisect him. Chang’s wuxia films used violence to attack simplistic notions of honor, but they still retain a hint of nobility wholly absent here as Shen grows ever more animalistic in his rampage through the gangsters’ ranks.

Kuei’s streetwise touch in the rawer, docudrama-like scenes of The Delinquent carries over to 1974’s The Teahouse and its 1975 sequel, Big Brother Cheng. Both films star Chen Kuan-tai as Brother Cheng, an immigrant restaurant manager whose community work primes him to become a protector when gangs threaten the peace. Gradually, Cheng inspires those he defends to forge a collective resistance against their assailants, flecking otherwise straightforward vigilante narratives with a kind of utopian communal solidarity. The action makes great use of cramped alleys and corridors as more and more attackers fill the frame for giant brawls.

Sun Chung’s Big Bad Sis spins off from the Brother Cheng films, this time shifting the focus to a factory where Ah-ying (Chen Ping) teaches her female co-workers martial arts so they can fend off the predations of men. You could call it a kung fu 9 to 5, at least in the lighter opening montages of the women learning self-defense techniques.

Quickly, however, the film turns dark and intense, showing in grim detail just how ruthless men can be in their unwanted pursuits. Crucially, it doesn’t pretend that newly trained women can suddenly fight like seasoned warriors, and the action often has a flailing desperation to it, even when it comes to Ah-ying, who’s frequently swarmed by gangsters from her mob past. Even the catharsis of watching these women knock their abusers down a peg is swallowed by the larger implications of just how embedded gendered violence is in the region.

Chen Kuan-tai makes yet another appearance as one of five bank robbers on the lam in Chor Yuen’s The Big Holdup. Intriguingly, the film gets its heist out of the way during the opening credits, devoting the rest of its running time to the rapid dissolution of honor among thieves. With only the occasional burst of chase action to break up scenes of expository backstory and bickering, the film moves at a lugubrious pace through a series of telegraphed betrayals.

Far better is Chor’s 1980 film The Convict Killer, which resembles a traditional Shaw Brothers wuxia in its early-20th-century setting and its use of soundstages and remote rural locations. In it, Teng (Ti Lung), recently released from prison after serving time for a crime he didn’t commit, seeks vengeance on the people responsible for his incarceration. In classic Shaw fashion, a straightforward plot rapidly spirals into convolution, with Teng forced to battle seven guardians of the mysterious figure who framed him. Nonetheless, Chor’s gorgeous anamorphic compositions and ample kung fu action override some of the confusion caused by the incessant twists and new characters, and the finale balances graceful choreography with palpable intensity as Teng barrels through every attempt to thwart his mission.

The finest balance between the studio’s bread-and-butter wuxia epics and its forays into modern grit can be found in Hua Shan’s 1979 film The Brothers. A remake of the Bollywood hit Deewaar, Hua’s film follows two close siblings (Tony Liu and Danny Lee) who grow up on opposite sides of the law and are bound to collide. It dials back the Shaw action in favor of the drama that besets the leads over the course of their lives, but where The Big Holdup feels sluggish and unfocused, The Brothers is compelling for its study of the social ills that are only glimpsed at the margins of the studio’s other contemporary crime films.

In the brothers’ childhood, we see their mother (Nam Hung) struggling to get by as a single parent amid wider epidemics of poverty and crime. Most notable today as a formative influence on John Woo’s A Better Tomorrow, and thus on the heroic bloodshed genre, Hua’s film is less flashy than Woo’s but shares many of its underlying preoccupations, namely the value of honor in the face of nihilism and the way moral codes can make unlikely allies of ostensible foes.

Each film comes from a new 2K restoration of the original 35mm negatives, and while Arrow makes the most of the available materials, image quality varies from title to title. Both Chor Yuen films, for example, are marked by frequent blurriness and soft detail that appear endemic to the negatives, while The Delinquent boasts sharper definition and richer color. Visible damage is minimal across the set, and given the location shooting of most of these films, lighting and textures remain fairly stable throughout each presentation. The lossless mono soundtracks, in Cantonese, Mandarin, and, for two of the films, English, are the usual blend of dubbed dialogue, music cues, and canned sound effects, with each element cleanly separated.

As usual, Arrow loads its latest trove of Shaw Brothers offerings with a healthy slate of extras. Each film gets a new audio commentary by one of the label’s regular Asian cinema experts: Frank Djeng handles The Delinquent, The Teahouse, Big Brother Cheng, and Big Bad Sis, James Mudge covers The Big Holdup and The Brothers, and David West takes on The Convict Killer. There are also new interviews with actors Susan Shaw and Chen Kuan-tai, the latter appearing both on his own and alongside Bruce Le. Djeng returns to discuss how The Brothers anticipated the heroic bloodshed films of the 1980s, and critic Tony Rayns, who died tragically in July at 77 after a fall in his home, surveys the filmographies of Chor Yuen and Kuei Chih-hung in a pair of interviews. Trailers and a booklet featuring new writing on the films by Jonathan Clements, Samm Deighan, Victor Fan, and David West round out the set.
Though not Shaw Brothers’ finest films, the crime dramas in Arrow’s latest set find the studio engaging with Hong Kong’s then-current anxieties and paving the way for future greatness.
